teaser: The title promises eight bridges. Count them, then ask where the story went.
review_notes:
The Met dates the screens 'after 1709'; the catalog year 1710 is an approximation.
Dimensions of each screen (about 164 x 352 cm) from the Met: check.
Kōrin's family business (the Kariganeya, textile merchants in Kyoto) and his spending of the inheritance: check.
Tarashikomi on the bridge planks: per the Met's description.
Hōitsu's 1815 woodblock book 'One Hundred Paintings by Kōrin': check.
The image is small (320 px high): the signatures are placed from the image but are only a few pixels wide.

lesson.text: Eight bridges in the title. One on the screens. And if you count the travelers, the river and the poet the story is about, you get zero each time. Ogata Kōrin has taken one of the best-known scenes in Japanese literature and deleted almost everything in it.

The scene comes from the Tales of Ise, a collection of poems and short episodes about a thousand years old. A nobleman, traveling far from the capital, stops at Yatsuhashi, the “Eight Bridges,” where a river splits into eight channels. Irises are blooming in the marsh, and he is homesick.

A companion dares the nobleman to write a poem in which each of the five lines begins with a syllable of the Japanese word for iris, ka-ki-tsu-ba-ta. He does, and the poem is about the wife he left behind. The whole party weeps into its rice.

Educated viewers in Kōrin's Japan knew this by heart. Irises plus a plank bridge was enough: their memory supplied the poet, the tears and the poem. So Kōrin could spend all his attention on the one thing left to design, the path across the gold.
The two screens stand side by side. Traditionally you read them from right to left.

lines.label: Coming down
lines.text: On the right screen the bridge enters from the top edge and drops in sharp angles. It is seen from above, almost like a plan.

lines.label: Leaving the frame
lines.text: It continues on the left screen, steps down again and exits at the bottom. Your eye has crossed the marsh in the traveler's place.

lines.label: The flowers' wave
lines.text: The tops of the iris clumps rise and fall like a line of music, playing against the hard zigzag of the planks.

lesson.text: That zigzag is the only straight-edged thing in the picture, and it slices across twelve panels as boldly as a pattern on a robe. This is no accident. Kōrin grew up in Kyoto in a family that ran a luxury textile shop, selling kimono fabrics to the ladies of the court.
Kōrin inherited a share of the family fortune at about thirty and spent it on pleasure within a few years. He turned to painting seriously in his late thirties, partly because he needed the money.

Each screen is about 164 cm high and 352 cm wide (roughly 5 ft 4 in by 11 ft 7 in), paper covered with squares of gold leaf, which is gold beaten thinner than a hair. Nothing tells you where the water is or where the sky starts. The gold is marsh, air and light at once.
Three ways of painting on the same gold, plus the artist's mark.

spots.title: Flowers without outlines
spots.text: The petals are patches of thick blue made from ground azurite, a mineral. No drawn contour holds them in. Lighter and darker blues suggest petals turning.

spots.title: Puddled planks
spots.text: On the bridge, Kōrin dripped ink and color into paint that was still wet and let it pool. The blotchy result, a technique called tarashikomi, reads as old, mossy wood.

spots.title: The grid of gold
spots.text: In the empty areas you can make out faint squares: the individual sheets of gold leaf, laid edge to edge by hand.

spots.title: Signature
spots.text: A short column of characters and a small seal sit alone on the bare gold of the right screen. A matching signature marks the far left of the other screen.

lesson.text: The leaves are a second mineral, green malachite, laid on in flat blades. Blue, green, gold and the gray of the bridge: four colors for about seven meters of painting. Screens like these stood on the floor of a room and were folded in a zigzag themselves, so the bridge would have bent with the panels.
Kōrin trusted his viewers to know the story, so he could leave it out. What remains is rhythm: a soft wave of flowers crossed by one hard broken line.

He had painted irises on gold once before, on a famous pair of screens now in the Nezu Museum in Tokyo, with no bridge at all. Returning to the subject some years later, he added the planks. The Metropolitan Museum bought this later pair in 1953.

Kōrin founded no school and had no direct line of pupils. A century after his death, the painter Sakai Hōitsu tracked down his works and published them in a woodblock-printed book. The style is now called Rinpa, “school of Rin,” after the last syllable of Kōrin's name.
Stand back from the gold one more time. A man once sat here, counted five syllables and missed his wife. Kōrin does not show him. He shows what the man was looking at when the poem came.

quiz.question: How many bridges actually appear on the screens?
quiz.explanation: A single plank bridge crosses both screens.

quiz.question: In the Tales of Ise, what was special about the poem written at Yatsuhashi?
options: Each line began with a syllable of the word for iris
It was carved on the bridge
It had eight lines, one per bridge
quiz.explanation: The five lines begin with ka, ki, tsu, ba, ta.

quiz.question: What was Kōrin's family business?
quiz.explanation: His family sold kimono fabrics in Kyoto.

quiz.question: What is tarashikomi?
options: Folding a screen in a zigzag
Dripping ink or color into wet paint so it pools
quiz.explanation: Kōrin used it on the planks of the bridge.

quiz.question: Where does the name Rinpa come from?
options: From the Japanese word for iris
From the last syllable of Kōrin's name

facts.text: Kōrin painted the homesick traveler crossing the bridge.
facts.explanation: No figure appears; viewers were expected to remember the story.

facts.text: The blue of the petals comes from a ground mineral, azurite.
facts.explanation: The petals are thick azurite blue, the leaves malachite green.

facts.text: The screens are meant to be read from left to right.
facts.explanation: Japanese screens are traditionally read from right to left.
